healthcareSystem: Two-tier system with public and private sectors. Tourists typically use private clinics. Public hospitals provide basic care.
qualityNotes: Private clinics in Tunis and coastal cities offer good quality care at reasonable prices. Tunisia is a regional hub for medical tourism. Public hospitals are adequate for emergencies but overcrowded. French is the medical language.
pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 8am-7pm Monday-Saturday; night pharmacies (pharmacie de nuit) available on rotation
pharmacyTips: Look for 'Pharmacie' signs with a green crescent or cross. Pharmacies are well-stocked and pharmacists are well-trained (French system). Many can provide medical advice. Communication in French and Arabic — some English in tourist areas.
prescriptionRules: French-style pharmacy regulations. Many common medications available OTC. Antibiotics officially require a prescription but enforcement can be lax. Controlled substances strictly require a prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: Controlled narcotics (opioids, tramadol)
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly controlled. Carry a doctor's letter and original prescription.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (benzodiazepines, stimulants)
restrictedMeds.note: Some psychiatric medications are controlled. Bring documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: Cannabis-based products
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal in all forms in Tunisia with severe penalties including imprisonment.

bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in French and English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, bring the original prescription. French-language documentation is preferred.

travelInsurance.tips: Travel insurance is recommended but Tunisia's private healthcare is affordable. Medical evacuation coverage is useful for serious conditions requiring transfer to France. Private clinics often accept direct billing from major international insurers.

recommended: Typhoid (for adventurous eaters or rural areas)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for entry from most countries. Yellow fever certificate required if arriving from an endemic country. Ensure routine vaccinations are current.

waterNotes: Tap water in Tunis and major cities is treated and generally safe, but bottled water is recommended for visitors to avoid stomach upset. In southern and rural areas, use bottled water.
foodSafetyTips: Tunisian cuisine is well-cooked and generally safe (couscous, brik, ojja, grilled fish). Be cautious with raw salads at budget eateries. Seafood on the coast is fresh and safe at established restaurants. Avoid tap water ice outside hotels.
medicalTourismNote: Tunisia is a significant medical tourism destination, especially for dental care, cosmetic surgery, ophthalmology, and orthopedics. Many clinics cater to European patients with competitive pricing and French-speaking staff.
metaDescription: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Tunisia. Emergency numbers, pharmacy tips, hospital info, medical tourism, and travel insurance advice.

dentalCare.availability: Excellent dental care available in Tunis and coastal cities. Tunisia is a major dental tourism destination.
dentalCare.costRange: $15-40 for a consultation; $20-60 for fillings; $15-40 for extractions; $200-400 per dental implant
dentalCare.notes: Tunisian dental clinics offer European-quality care at significantly lower prices. Many dentists trained in France. Dental tourism packages available including hotel stays.
dentalCare.emergencyTip: For dental emergencies, visit a private dental clinic (cabinet dentaire). In tourist areas like Sousse and Hammamet, hotel reception can recommend nearby dentists.

mentalHealth.internationalLine: No dedicated English-language crisis line — contact your embassy
mentalHealth.englishTherapists: Limited. French-speaking therapists widely available in Tunis. Some may speak English.
mentalHealth.notes: Mental health services in French are available in Tunis. English services are rare. Mental health awareness is growing but stigma remains.

accessibilityInfo.overview: Accessibility infrastructure is limited but improving in newer developments. Historic medinas and older areas are very challenging.
accessibilityInfo.hospitalAccess: Private clinics are generally wheelchair accessible. Public hospitals vary in accessibility.
accessibilityInfo.transport: Public transport has limited accessibility. Taxis are the most practical option. The Tunis light rail has some accessible stations.
accessibilityInfo.tips: Tunisia's medinas (old towns) and archaeological sites have uneven terrain. Beach resorts in Hammamet and Sousse tend to have better accessibility. Request accessible rooms in advance.

covidStatus.entryRequirements: No COVID testing or vaccination requirements for entry as of 2026.
covidStatus.maskPolicy: No mask mandates. Masks may be requested in healthcare facilities.
covidStatus.testing: Tests available at private labs and pharmacies (rapid tests). PCR tests at private labs in Tunis.
covidStatus.notes: All COVID entry restrictions have been lifted.

insuranceClaimProcess: Private clinics may accept direct billing from major international insurers. Otherwise, pay upfront (cash in Tunisian dinar or euros, cards accepted at larger clinics). Keep all receipts and documentation in French. File claims upon return.

commonCosts.note: Estimated typical out-of-pocket costs at private facilities. Tunisia offers excellent value healthcare. Medical tourism procedures are significantly cheaper than in Europe.

medicalEvacuation.note: Tunisia's private hospitals handle most conditions well. Evacuation to France is the standard route for specialized care. Air ambulance to Europe is relatively short (2-3 hours).
